description: Solo team building a realistic Unreal Engine Marswalk planner: a hyperlocal, layered 3D map of one Martian site with a safe walking route and hazard info, streamed to the browser.
summary: Marswalk is a hyperlocal map and mission simulator for one astronaut excursion on Mars: a 2 km by 2 km piece of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, where Curiosity explored boxwork ridges in 2025. The science goal is to sample a ridge and the hollow beside it to learn how long groundwater flowed there. We layered five NASA data types on the ground: HiRISE 1 m elevation and 25 cm imagery, THEMIS thermal inertia, and Curiosity's RAD radiation and REMS weather records. From them we planned a 2.0 km walking loop for a suited astronaut that avoids slopes over 20 degrees and blocky rock, visiting four places where Curiosity drilled or imaged, each with its own Navcam photo. It runs in Unreal Engine 5.8 and streams to a browser. In the habitat the crew sees a plan view; on the walk a helmet HUD shows bearing, slope, oxygen, radiation dose and daylight left. A solar-storm event replays the May 2024 dose Curiosity measured and prices the choice to turn back. Marswalk gives a first Mars crew one trustworthy view of where to walk, what it costs in time and radiation, and when to go home.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. Marswalk is one astronaut excursion, planned and played on real Mars data. The site is 2 km by 2 km of Mount Sharp in Gale crater (lat -4.808, lon 137.3815), where Curiosity explored boxwork ridges in 2025. The science goal is to drill a ridge and the hollow beside it to learn how long groundwater flowed there. The brief asks for a layered view of one place, not a global map, so everything is built for a person on foot in a suit.

DATA LAYERS (five types). Topography: HiRISE 1 m stereo elevation model. Optical: HiRISE 25 cm orthoimage. Thermal: THEMIS thermal inertia (sandier vs firmer ground). Radiation: Curiosity RAD surface dose, quiet day and the 20 May 2024 solar storm. Atmosphere: Curiosity REMS temperature, pressure, UV, sunrise and sunset. A layer key switches the ground between image, slope, thermal inertia and hazards.

THE ROUTE. Each 1 m cell costs walking time: 0.7 m/s on flat ground, Tobler's hiking function for slope, up to 30 percent slower on sandy ground. No-go cells are slopes over 20 degrees or more than 0.5 m of rock or ledge relief (29 percent of the site). Dijkstra links the habitat and four stops, then the path is straightened wherever a straight line stays 1 m clear of no-go cells. Result: a 2.04 km loop, 112 m of climb, steepest step 19.7 degrees, 65 min of walking plus 4 x 30 min at stops, about 3.1 h out. A built-in check confirms every step is out of no-go cells and the loop closes. The four stops are places Curiosity really drilled or imaged (sols 4628, 4693, 4718, 4855), each with that rover's own Navcam photo as a "what to expect" view.

THE MISSION. A brief in the habitat gives the science goal, route, oxygen, dose limit and daylight. Outside, a helmet-visor HUD shows a line on the ground to the next stop, bearing and distance, slope underfoot, and oxygen, dose and daylight bars. At each stop the walker drills a core and can photograph the outcrop beside Curiosity's own frame. After the second core a solar storm arrives at the dose rate Curiosity measured in May 2024 (8.1 mGy in the event, against 0.027 mGy for this EVA on a quiet day, 1.04 mGy in a storm), and the HUD prices the choice: the dose for walking home now against the dose for each further core. Back at the airlock the walker can refill, wait out the storm inside, go out again, or end the mission. A debrief scores cores, dose against the limit, oxygen left and daylight. The habitat screen shows the plan view with route numbers, dose and weather.

HOW IT IS BUILT. GDAL reprojects the HiRISE DTM, orthoimage and THEMIS mosaic onto one 1 m grid. Python (NumPy, SciPy) computes slope over a 3 m baseline (HiRISE stereo resolves about 3 m), roughness and the route. Unreal Engine 5.8 turns the DTM into Nanite terrain with collision on the real surface, one material that blends the data layers, a Mars sky (thin CO2 plus dust, optical depth about 0.6) with the Sun placed from the site latitude and solar declination, Mars gravity of 3.71 m/s2, and 74,000 scanned rocks placed where the DTM is rough. Pixel Streaming 2 sends the view to a browser. The scene build and HUD logic are Python inside Unreal, the HUD layout is a UMG widget, and the project has no C++.

IMPACT AND LIMITS. A first crew will need to answer "where do we walk, what does it cost, and when do we turn back" from one view. Marswalk shows that answer from real orbital and rover data, and lets a planner rehearse the decision before it matters. Suit pace (0.7 m/s), slope limit (20 degrees), rock limit (0.5 m), sand slowdown (30 percent), 4 h of oxygen, a 250 microgray dose rule and 30 min per core are stated planning assumptions, not measurements. THEMIS is 100 m per pixel, so it marks sandier vs firmer ground at that scale only. HiRISE cannot see rocks smaller than about 3 m; the clasts beside the route are placed for scale, not mapped. The mission clock runs as a 10x time-lapse while walking.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE (AI) USE. The code in this project (data pipeline, route planner, Unreal build scripts, HUD logic) and the README were written with an AI coding assistant, Anthropic's Claude, directed and reviewed by the team. All data are NASA and NASA-partner measurements. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used; the demo video is a screen capture of the running Unreal scene. Third-party assets (Poly Haven CC0 rock and ground scans, NASA's Curiosity 3D model, Unreal template content) and every dataset and tool are listed in the fields below and in DATA.md in the repository.
